title: AK Fall 2-2: Layered Glacier River Editing in Photoshop from Aerial Footage

date.basis: Embedded file creation time 2025-09-18 and folder naming hint at the 2024–2025 production window.

locations.name: Alaska (probable)
locations.basis: Transcript repeatedly references Alaska and a Badlands analogue set in Alaska; the exact shooting location is not explicitly confirmed.

summary: The video presents a field-to-desk workflow for transforming dramatic glacier-river imagery into polished landscape photographs using Photoshop. The speaker walks through a sequence of practical edits on aerial/frontal glacier river shots, starting with aggressive shadow recovery and controlled exposure to preserve subtle details in glacial depths, then progressively shaping tonal contrast and color to emphasize depth and atmosphere. A core emphasis is the separation of image layers—especially sky, midground, and foreground—to create directional light and three-dimensionality, aided by dehaze, clarity, texture, and selective color adjustments. The tutorial demonstrates hands-on techniques for cropping to create focal points, faking missing river detail with cloning when needed, and applying staged color grades to produce fall colors while keeping natural balance. A distinctive portion explains the beam-creation technique using dehaze and painting, and another section covers perspective correction (warping) to preserve natural edges while enhancing layer separation. Throughout, the presenter discusses practical constraints (time, equipment like the Pro 3 drone and its storage, shutter choices like F4 vs F11) and emphasizes the painterly quality of “rock abstracts” and layered formations that define the composition. The video also references broader workflow concepts such as HDR exposure tuning, tonal-based color adjustments, and the importance of intentional composition over simply accumulating visually striking elements. Overall, the content offers a compact, repeatable set of Photoshop techniques for turning highly textured glacier landscapes into cinematic, multi-layered images.

sections.title: Initial tonal adjustments and shadow recovery
sections.description: Begins with basic tonal balancing on glacial river imagery, emphasizing shadow detail recovery and early decisions about how much to suppress highlights before pulling up luminosity. The presenter notes the natural whiteness versus darker areas and demonstrates two passes of shadow/black adjustments to set a flat base for subsequent edits.

sections.title: Layer separation concept and sky/midground emphasis
concepts: color temp and whites toward directionality
sections.description: Proceedes to separate image layers, first by dehazing and then by selectively painting separation masks to create distinct sky, midground, and foreground layers. The technique emphasizes enhancing directional light from a specific side, adjusting whites and color temperature, and using brushes to refine edges for natural layering.

sections.title: Color tuning, fall color, and foreground emphasis
sections.description: Demonstrates mass and selective color techniques to introduce fall color while maintaining natural balance. The workflow includes greens/yellows adjustments, tint considerations, and painting fall tones into strategic regions to guide the viewer’s eye toward the river and light patterns.

sections.title: Rock abstracts and canyon/rock glacier considerations
sections.description: Discusses using painterly rock patterns and abstract crops to highlight textures and layers. The presenter explains selecting strong abstract elements and refining texture with white adjustments to balance contrast and depth.

sections.title: Atmosphere, beams, and atmospheric separation
sections.description: Focuses on maximizing atmosphere by enhancing layer separation and introducing light beams. The beam creation technique is demonstrated with dehaze and painted beams, including guidance on angle, hardness, and erasing overlaps. Talks about using weather and fog to create natural separation and drama.
